title: Agentic AI Vendor Evaluation: Healthcare Guide | Snowflake
summary: Evaluate agentic AI vendors with Snowflake's 13-point framework for healthcare and life sciences. Download the enterprise evaluation today.
body_markdown:
Navigating an agentic AI vendor evaluation in healthcare and life sciences requires balancing technical innovation with regulatory requirements. Unlike traditional predictive models, autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents execute actions directly across clinical trials, provider operations, patient services, and claims management.


Use this 13-point architectural framework to help CEOs, CTOs, CDOs and other executive decision-makers evaluate vendor data readiness, governance boundaries, multi-model flexibility, and verifiable business ROI.


### 1. Does the solution support our highest-priority business workflows and products?


The solution should align to real business processes, not just broad AI capabilities. You should evaluate whether the platform can support the workflows that matter most to the organization, such as customer experience, operations, product development, risk management, revenue growth, cost reduction or employee productivity.


A strong vendor should be able to show how its solution moves from narrow use cases to more complex agentic workflows over time.


### 2. Is our data estate AI ready — and can the solution work where our data already lives?


AI agents are only as effective as the data they can access. The solution should work with structured, unstructured and semi-structured data that is readable, harmonized and governed.


You should look for solutions that process data where it already lives, instead of requiring teams to move sensitive data into separate AI environments or build complex data-to-AI pipelines. This reduces migration risk, cost, complexity and time to value.


### 3. Does the solution support enterprise-grade AI experiences for both business users and technical builders?


Agentic AI should create value across the organization, not only for technical teams. The solution should provide business users with ready-to-use conversational experiences for discovering insights, while also giving developers, data engineers and data scientists the tools to build, customize and extend agents. The solution should use a shared semantic layer so all groups work from the same metrics, and let teams extend agents with custom tools rather than only configure packaged agents.


This helps close the gap between AI builders and AI users while keeping both groups within the same security and governance framework.


### 4. How flexible is the solution when it comes to model choice and AI vendor selection?


AI model performance, cost, latency and capabilities change quickly, so you should avoid being locked into a single model, provider or proprietary approach. The platform should provide native access to a broad range of foundation models and specialized agentic tools from multiple providers, allowing teams to choose the best model or AI service for each use case based on performance, cost, latency and business requirements.


Look for solutions that make model and vendor flexibility part of the platform itself, rather than requiring internal teams to manage separate deployments, API integrations or custom connectivity. This gives the organization the ability to adapt as the AI ecosystem evolves while reducing integration burden, complexity and lock-in.


### 5. Can the solution apply AI across all relevant data types, formats and volumes?


AI value should not be limited by data type, data domain or data volume. The solution should work across structured, semi-structured, unstructured and multimodal data, including text, documents, images, audio, video, logs, events and other business-critical data sources.


The platform should allow organizations to apply AI to the full breadth of their enterprise data, not only to narrow use cases involving structured warehouse data or natural language processing. This gives teams more room to innovate, uncover new use cases and scale AI across domains without fragmenting data, duplicating infrastructure or constraining what agents can analyze and act on.


### 6. Does the solution integrate data and AI services on a unified platform?


A unified data and AI platform can reduce fragmentation, simplify governance and accelerate delivery. When data and AI services are separated across multiple tools, teams often need to build complex pipelines, duplicate data and manage inconsistent controls.


You should look for a platform that brings together AI services, tools, compute infrastructure, governance, cost management and observability in one integrated environment.


### 7. How does the solution enforce governed data access?


The same permissions, access controls, privacy rules, lineage, auditability and compliance policies that govern enterprise data should also extend to AI agents.


This is especially important because agents may retrieve information, generate recommendations or take action across workflows. Unified governance across data and AI helps reduce risk, avoid policy gaps and build trust with business, compliance and security stakeholders.


### 8. Does our data stay within our secure, governed boundary at all times?


You should understand whether the solution processes data in place or requires sensitive data to leave the organization’s secure environment.


The architecture should help you ensure data remains protected, governed and controlled, even when the platform uses AI models or services from multiple vendors. This is critical for managing privacy, regulatory, security and reputational risk.


### 9. Can we define what agents are allowed to do and where human review is required?


Enterprise AI agents need clear boundaries. The solution should allow the organization to define levels of autonomy, approval workflows, escalation paths and human review requirements.


You should look for controls that ensure agents operate within approved limits and that people remain accountable for high-impact decisions. This is essential for scaling AI responsibly.


### 10. How transparent and auditable are agent actions and outputs?


The organization should be able to understand what an agent did, why it acted, which data or tools it used and how it generated an output.


Comprehensive auditability controls support compliance, risk management, quality assurance and executive trust. It also gives teams the visibility needed to investigate issues, improve performance and document responsible AI practices.


### 11. Can the solution measure agent performance against business outcomes?


You should avoid evaluating agentic AI only by technical performance or pilot success. The solution should help measure business impact, including productivity, cycle time, quality, cost reduction, customer experience, revenue growth or risk reduction.


The best solutions support continuous improvement by analyzing interactions, monitoring performance and helping teams refine agents over time.


### 12. How easy is it to test, refine and scale agents over time?


The vendor should make it possible to start with focused, lower-risk use cases and expand responsibly. You should look for a clear path from experimentation to production, including testing, monitoring, governance, iteration and scale.


A strong platform should support both early pilots and more advanced multi-agent workflows as the organization’s maturity grows.


### 13. What support, expertise and implementation guidance does the vendor provide?


The vendor should be more than a technology provider. You should evaluate whether the vendor can support workflow design, data readiness, governance, change management and production deployment.


Strong vendors provide quickstarts, reference architectures, best practices and real-world customer examples that help organizations reduce risk and accelerate time to value.
